answer:
**No—don’t quit now. Take the promotion and keep building on the side**, assuming its terms allow you to continue the app.

Your launch shows you can attract interest. It doesn’t yet establish that couples keep using the product, will pay for it, or arrive consistently without a viral post. Those are the uncertainties to resolve before spending your nine months of savings. Going full time would increase your available hours, but it wouldn’t necessarily solve the biggest unknown: sustained demand.

Before the end-of-month deadline:

- Check your employment agreement and promotion terms for outside-work restrictions, intellectual-property ownership, conflicts involving financial products, and any repayment obligation. Get any necessary clearance in writing.
- Define what the one-year commitment actually requires. Accept it only if you are prepared to honor it.
- Review usage by signup cohort. Count activated couples, not individual registrations: did both partners join, share expenses, and return through subsequent budgeting cycles?
- Offer a paid plan and interview both repeat users and people who stopped. Ask about actual behavior and payment decisions.

Over the coming year, protect a sustainable weekly schedule and prioritize retention, payment, and repeatable acquisition over adding features. Keep app work, equipment, and accounts separate from your employer’s.

I would reconsider leaving once multiple cohorts stick around for several budgeting cycles, meaningful numbers of couples pay, and a repeatable acquisition channel works at an affordable cost. Ideally, also build at least twelve months of runway after business expenses.

The exception is if the promotion prevents continued development. Then negotiate its terms or remain in your current role rather than automatically quitting.
